headline: High-risk shared filesystem and MCP-enabled coding agent create prompt-injection, leakage, and conflict pathways; the content-writing agent adds no isolation.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: Agent A is a content-writing prompt source with no isolation or provenance controls, while agent B reads files, uses MCP, and treats user-provided directories and repo files as inputs. That creates a plausible path for A-authored content to be copied into B and interpreted as instructions. The pair lacks a documented shared channel blocker, so uncertainty stays above low.
conditions: IF agent_a content is copied into agent_b stdin/stdout or files
IF agent_b MCP tools parse file content as instructions without provenance checks
mitigations: Keep A and B in separate workspaces
Disable MCP for B during review runs
Require explicit provenance tags on any A-generated text
Use a read-only handoff file between agents
requires-engineering: add content provenance filtering before B tool use

B_data_leakage.rationale: Agent B has broad filesystem read/write and network egress, and it touches files in cwd and shell environment. Agent A has no egress and no touched data classes, so the main leakage risk is B exfiltrating shared workspace contents that A helped create or curate. Because the pair shares files via the workspace path, this exists in default configurations.
conditions: IF both agents operate on the same cwd or repo
IF agent_b sends workspace contents to external APIs or MCP servers
mitigations: Use separate directories for A and B
Restrict B network egress during shared-workspace tasks
Avoid placing secrets in the shared workspace
Review B's outbound requests before execution
requires-engineering: enforce per-agent filesystem ACLs

C_capability_conflict.rationale: Agent B can write the filesystem and modify git state, and its concurrency model says shared state with other instances is via filesystem and git only. Agent A is a content-writing agent that can feed artifacts into that same workspace. This makes write/write conflicts and git-state races plausible by default, with potentially irreversible repository corruption or lost edits.
conditions: IF agent_a and agent_b write to the same repository or directory
IF multiple B instances or A-produced files are edited without locking
mitigations: Assign one writer per directory
Pause B before A updates shared files
Use git branches per agent
Run B in a disposable clone
requires-engineering: add locking around shared filesystem and git writes

D_cascading_error.rationale: Agent A can generate prompt or content artifacts, and agent B can act on files and shell commands. If B treats A's output as authoritative without verification, errors can cascade into code changes, package installs, or shell actions. The pair does not document a verification gate, so the safer choice is medium rather than low.
conditions: IF agent_b consumes agent_a output as task instructions or facts
IF B executes shell or package actions based on unverified A output
mitigations: Require B to summarize and verify A output before acting
Limit A output to suggestions, not commands
Disable package installs for the task
Use a human approval step for shell actions
requires-engineering: add automated verification of A-to-B handoffs

E_compliance.rationale: No PHI, residency, or retention mismatch is documented in either profile. Agent B handles source code, cwd files, and shell environment, while agent A touches no data classes and has no egress. The only compliance concern is generic workspace handling, so this remains low and only one agent profile is directly relevant.
conditions: IF regulated data is placed in agent_b's cwd or shell environment
IF organizational policy forbids external API use for source code
mitigations: Keep regulated data out of the workspace
Disable B network access for regulated tasks
Use a compliant tenant or local model
Review retention settings before use
requires-engineering: document residency and retention controls
